learning_objectives: Students will describe how changing the number of rubber bands may affect the catapult’s motion, using observations as evidence.
Students will compare how changing the supplied ball’s position relates to the catapult’s motion and explain one design choice using evidence.
Students will record a simple test, identify what was changed, and distinguish an observation from a prediction.
classroom_preparation: On paper, make a two-column chart labeled “I predict” and “I observed,” plus space to note what was changed between tests.
Review that students should follow museum staff directions for all catapult handling and testing; do not add or substitute objects.
background_concepts: A force is a push or pull that can change an object’s motion.
In a test, changing one factor at a time can help make comparisons clearer; observations describe what happened, while hypotheses are testable explanations or predictions.
inquiry_questions: How might changing the number of rubber bands affect the catapult’s motion?
How might the supplied ball’s position affect its motion when launched?
What evidence would help us decide whether a design change made a difference?

observation_prompts: If permitted by museum staff, invite students to notice the number of bands, the ball’s position, and what happens during each staff-directed test.
Ask students to observe how the motion changes between comparisons, without handling or adjusting equipment unless staff direct them.
hypothesis_questions: Before a staff-directed comparison, what do you predict will happen if the number of bands changes? Why?
What do you predict may change when the supplied ball is placed in a different position? What makes you think so?
critical_thinking: Which factor changed between the tests being compared? Did anything else appear to change?
Did the observation match your prediction? What might explain a difference?
What can this test tell us, and what would require another comparison?
evidence_collection: On paper, record the test condition described by staff and a brief observation of the resulting motion.
Use words or a simple sketch to compare two staff-directed tests; record whether the prediction matched the observation.
Follow museum staff instructions for all equipment procedures and use only the supplied ball as directed.

reflection_questions: Which change seemed related to a difference in motion? What observation supports your answer?
When did the result differ from your prediction, and how did you revise your thinking?
What would you change in a next test to make the comparison clearer? Explain your choice.
after.follow_up_activity: On paper, draw or describe a catapult test as a simple before-and-after comparison. Identify one factor to change, write a prediction, and add a made-up observation clearly labeled as an example; do not build or launch a device.
assessment: Objective 1: Check whether each student describes a possible relationship between band count and motion and cites an observation from their notes.
Objective 2: Check whether each student compares ball positions and explains a design choice using an observed result.
Objective 3: Review the test record for a clearly identified changed factor, a prediction, and a distinct observation.
after.extension_activity: Students can use a paper-and-pencil table to propose a follow-up comparison that changes one factor, predict a result, and explain what observation would support or challenge the prediction.
